title: Dashboard Requirements Document
description: The requirements document that prevents you building the wrong dashboard. Six sections, fits on one page. Read once with the stakeholder; signed off before any SQL is written. The discipline is asking 'what decision does this support' until the answer is specific enough to build against.
empty_template_md:
# [Dashboard name] — Requirements
_Requestor: [name] · audience: [primary user(s)] · DA: [you] · target date: [date]_

## 1. Decision this supports
_What decision (or set of decisions) does the user need to make using this dashboard? Specific. 'Where to focus the team's effort this week' is OK; 'see how sales is doing' is not._

## 2. Primary user + cadence
_Who opens this most. How often (daily / weekly / monthly / one-off). The opening cadence shapes the entire design._

## 3. The metrics
_Three to seven metrics. Each one: name, business definition (plain English), SQL definition (one line), slicing dimensions, refresh cadence. Anything beyond seven and the dashboard becomes a directory._

## 4. Slicing dimensions
_The 2-4 dimensions users will slice by (e.g. segment, region, channel, time grain). If they want fifteen slicing dimensions, the actual ask is a self-serve query tool, not a dashboard._

## 5. What this dashboard is NOT for
_The boundary section. What this dashboard explicitly will not answer. Saves three months of 'can we also add X'._

## 6. Success criteria
_How we'll know the dashboard is being used. Specific. 'Daniel opens it on Monday mornings' is testable; 'it's useful' is not._

worked_examples.title: Sales pipeline dashboard — requirements with Daniel Quigley
worked_examples.content_md:
# Sales Pipeline Dashboard — Requirements
_Requestor: Daniel Quigley (Head of Sales) · audience: Daniel + his director (Tobi Adesanya) · DA: [you] · target date: 8 May 2026_

## 1. Decision this supports

Weekly: Daniel decides where to push sales effort the following week — which segments are underperforming, which deals are slipping, which channels are working. Monthly: Daniel's QBR conversation with Tobi needs a defensible pipeline-velocity view by segment.

## 2. Primary user + cadence

- **Primary:** Daniel, opens it Monday mornings (9-10am) and during weekly sales-leadership stand-up Wednesdays.
- **Secondary:** Tobi, looks at it before monthly 1:1 with Daniel.
- **Not the user:** the broader Sales team. They have CRM-native views.

## 3. The metrics

| Metric | Plain English | SQL definition | Slicing | Refresh |
|--------|---------------|----------------|---------|---------|
| Pipeline value | Sum of open-deal value at current stage | `sum(amount) where stage in ('discovery','proposal','negotiation')` | segment, channel, week | Daily |
| Stage velocity | Median days to move stage-to-stage | `median(days_in_stage) where stage transitions in last 90d` | segment, stage | Weekly |
| Conversion rate | % of deals entering Discovery that close-won | `won / entered_discovery` by entry-week | segment, channel | Weekly |
| At-risk deals | Deals >2× median time in current stage | rule-based — TBD with Daniel | segment, owner | Daily |

## 4. Slicing dimensions

- Segment (Enterprise / Mid-market / SMB)
- Channel (Direct / Partner / Inbound)
- Time grain (this week, this month, this quarter, custom)
- Deal owner (defaults off — turn on only for the deep-dive view)

## 5. What this dashboard is NOT for

- Individual rep performance reviews (sits with Sales leadership separately).
- Forecasting (separate model owned by Finance).
- CRM data quality (a different conversation; this dashboard assumes upstream data is OK).
- Deal-level commentary or notes (the CRM is the system of record for that).

## 6. Success criteria

- Daniel opens the dashboard at least 3 of 4 Mondays in May.
- Daniel uses at least one specific dashboard view in his weekly Wednesday stand-up.
- After 4 weeks, neither Daniel nor Tobi has asked you to add a new metric (i.e. the original set is doing the job).
- Tobi cites the dashboard in his next monthly 1:1 with Daniel.

annotations.note: Decision-this-supports section is the heart of the document. If you can't fill it in, the dashboard shouldn't be built. The stakeholder will give you a vague answer; your job is to keep asking until it's specific.
Three to seven metrics. More than seven and the dashboard becomes a directory; nobody can hold the picture in their head. The discipline is in the cut.
What-this-is-NOT-for section saves you the 'can we also add forecasting?' conversation in week 4. Always include it. Three to five items minimum.

Success criteria with named users opening the dashboard at named cadences. 'It's useful' is not a success criterion. Without observable criteria, you can't tell whether the dashboard is doing its job.

common_mistakes: Skipping the requirements doc because 'it'll slow things down'. The dashboard will be wrong, abandoned, or both — and the requirements conversation will have to happen anyway, later, retroactively, with worse data.
Metrics that aren't decision-anchored. 'Total signups' is a metric. 'Net new paid customers by week, used to decide whether to extend the partner-channel investment' is a decision-anchored metric.
More than seven metrics. The dashboard becomes a directory; users skim and stop using it.
Slicing dimensions without limits. 'Slice by anything' is not a dashboard; it's a self-serve query tool. If that's what the user actually wants, name it and build it differently.
Success criteria omitted. Without observable adoption criteria, you'll never know whether the dashboard is being used; you'll only know when someone complains it's wrong.
Requirements doc written by the DA alone and emailed for sign-off. The conversation IS the requirements doc. The signed doc is just the record.
variant_patterns: Executive-dashboard variant: §3 becomes ≤4 metrics. §5 (what this is NOT for) grows — executives need very tight scoping. §6 includes 'mentioned by name in the next board pack'.
Operational-dashboard variant (used hourly / daily by an operations team): §2 cadence shifts; §3 includes alert thresholds; §6 includes 'used to action a decision in the last 24 hours'.
One-off-analysis variant (not really a dashboard): collapse to §1 + §3 only. If the user only needs the answer once, build a one-pager, not a dashboard.
